newsitem.title: USA: US might need 20,000 bpd heating oil imports - API.
newsitem.headline: US might need 20,000 bpd heating oil imports - API.

text.p: Even if this winter is no colder than normal, the United States is expected to need 20,000 barrels per day of heating oil imports from October through March, according to the American Petroleum Institute.

U.S. heating oil demand should reach 3.47 million bpd, up from 3.44 bpd last winter, assuming normal winter temperatures and modest economic growth, according to the oil industry group's winter outlook to be released next week, an API spokesman said.
To meet the demand, refinery production would have to reach 3.285 million bpd, with imports averaging 20,000 bpd and stockdraws averaging 165,000 bpd, according to the API scenario.
The winter outlook comes at a time when heating oil prices have been near five-year highs and the U.S. Energy Information Administration has been pointing to low heating oil stocks in the Northeast.
But the API spokesman said that "inventories are adequate to meet draws of nearly 300,000 bpd during the height of the season (at its coldest point)."

By comparison, the Energy Information Administration's last published outlook saw distillate demand for this winter reaching 3.45 million bpd, which would be met with refinery output of 3.285 million bpd, imports of 20,000 bpd and stockdraws of 145,000 bpd.
In both API and EIA's scenarios, the expected stockdraws are lower than they were during last year's severe winter, when inventories were drained at an average 230,000 bpd.
At the same time, both API and EIA see imports at much higher levels than last winter's 7,000 bpd.
U.S. government officials said this week they were watching the stock situation but added that it was too early to tell whether supplies were too low.

EIA this week warned that U.S. distillate stocks were about 20 million barrels below normal for this time of the year, with East Coast stocks of 39 million barrels more than 17 million barrels lower than a year ago.
"There's a yellow flag up," said Deputy Energy Secretary Charles Curtis. "We're trusting that the market will make the requisite adjustment here."
"I don't think anybody's panicking yet by any means," said a White House official, but added that the industry should be careful not to let supplies drop too low.

"When the stock levels are as low as they are now, it is appropriate for not only elected officials to take note and raise their concerns about it, but it's also appropriate for the industry to understand that they're risking a political reaction if they don't respond in responsible fashion and time frame," he said.
